chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, and Muhammad ibn Yahya from Talhah ibn Zayd, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The polytheists raided the pasture area of Medina, and an announcer cried out in it: 'How bad is this morning!' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) heard it while among the cavalry, so he mounted his horse in pursuit of the enemy. The first of his companions to reach him was Abu Qatadah on his horse. The saddle of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) had two pads made of palm fiber, containing no extravagance or pride. They pursued the enemy but found no one, and the cavalry followed one after another. Abu Qatadah said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the enemy has departed; if you see fit, let us race.' He said: 'Yes.' They raced, and the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) emerged as the winner among them. Then he turned to them and said: 'I am the son of the three 'Awatik women of Quraysh; indeed, it is al-Jawad al-Bahr,' meaning his horse.

key_terms.الْجَوَاد الْبَحْر: The fine horse that runs widely (like the sea)

ai.seo_question: What does the Prophet's horse name 'al-Jawad al-Bahr' signify in this narration?
ai.summary: This narration from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the Prophet’s (peace be upon him) martial readiness and humility, contrasting the simplicity of his saddle (*sarg*) with the nobility of his horse, *al-Jawad al-Bahr*. It serves as a foundational text for the virtue of horsemanship in Shia tradition, emphasizing that physical prowess should be coupled with modesty and readiness for jihad. The event underscores the practical application of spiritual virtues in the context of early Islamic military campaigns.
